scenario: The team receives about 140 alert emails a week, mostly CPU above 70% on individual App Service instances. Everyone filters them unread.
options: Raise the CPU threshold to 90%
Page only on user-facing symptoms such as checkout error rate, latency and availability; move CPU to dashboards or working-hours tickets
Send the alerts by SMS instead of email
Add more alerts so nothing is missed
explanation: High CPU is a cause that may or may not hurt anyone; symptom alerts fire only when users are affected. Fewer, meaningful alerts get read. A higher threshold still pages on causes, SMS just moves the noise to phones, and more alerts deepen the fatigue.

stem: Checkout's SLO is 99.5% good requests over 30 days. What is the error budget, roughly, in time?
options: About 36 minutes a month
About 3.6 hours a month
About 36 hours a month
There is no budget; any failure breaks the SLO
explanation: 0.5% of 30 days (720 hours) is 3.6 hours of equivalent full failure. The budget is what the SLO allows to go wrong; spending it quickly is what burn-rate alerts detect.

stem: Why set an internal SLO tighter than the SLA published to customers?
options: SLAs are only for Azure services
So the team sees and fixes reliability problems before customers are owed service credits
Because SLOs are measured monthly and SLAs yearly
To make dashboards look better
explanation: The SLA is a contractual promise with penalties; the SLO is the working target. A tighter SLO gives warning and room to act before the contractual line is crossed.

scenario: During an Azure App Service incident in UK South, Azure's notification went to the email of a contractor who created the subscription two years ago.
options: Nothing; Azure incidents are Microsoft's responsibility
Service Health alerts for the shop's services and regions, routed to the on-call action group
A daily check of the Azure status web page
Resource locks on the App Service
explanation: Azure's problems still become your incidents. Service Health alerts scoped to your services and regions, delivered through the on-call action group, reach the people who can fail over or communicate. A status page checked by hand is too slow, and locks have nothing to do with it.

scenario: Every Tuesday-night release pages the on-call engineer with expected errors during the slot swap.
options: Disable the alert rules on Tuesdays by hand
An alert processing rule that suppresses notifications for the release window, with a defined end
Delete the checkout alerts
Lower the alert severity permanently
explanation: Alert processing rules suppress notifications for a scope and time window, then stop by themselves. Disabling rules by hand risks forgetting to re-enable them, and deleting or downgrading alerts removes protection for the other 167 hours of the week.

stem: Why alert on error-budget burn rate rather than on any single failed checkout?
options: Single failures cannot be detected
Burn rate separates outages, which spend the budget fast and need a page, from slow leaks, which need attention but not at 3am, while ignoring normal background errors
Burn-rate alerts are free
Azure only supports burn-rate alerts
explanation: Every system has some failures. Measuring how quickly the budget is being spent - fast burn over an hour, slow burn over six - matches the urgency of the page to the damage being done. Alerting on each failure recreates alert fatigue.

scenario: An alert pages the on-call engineer at 03:00 with the text 'DLQ count > 0'. She has never seen it before.
options: A higher severity
A runbook linked from the alert: what it means, what to check first, how to mitigate and whom to call
A second alert for the same condition
An SMS as well as the push notification
explanation: An alert should tell a stranger at 3am what to do. The runbook turns a cryptic signal into steps, starting with the workbook and the dead-letter reasons. More severity or more notifications only make an unexplained alert louder.

stem: Which habit keeps an alert set healthy over time?
options: Adding a new alert after every incident and never removing any
A weekly review of every alert that fired: actionable ones stay, noisy ones are tuned or deleted, and pages per shift are tracked
Letting each developer create alerts to their own email
Reviewing alerts once a year
explanation: Alert sets rot: traffic changes, services change, and noise creeps back. A regular review keeps each alert meaningful and the on-call load humane. Only adding alerts, or routing them to individuals, is how the 140-email week happened.
